questions.q: The right to practice law in India, exercised by an advocate, is generally regarded as:
o: An absolute, unqualified right with no possible restriction whatsoever

A valuable right protected under Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution (right to practise any profession), but one that is subject to reasonable restrictions, including those imposed by the Advocates Act 1961 and Bar Council rules
A right that can never be regulated by any statute
Only a privilege granted by individual courts, with no constitutional basis at all
questions.src: Constitution of India, Article 19(1)(g) — the right to practise a profession (including law) is protected but subject to reasonable restrictions under Article 19(6) and the regulatory framework of the Advocates Act 1961

questions.q: The Advocates Act, 1961 was enacted primarily to:
o: Abolish the legal profession in India

Amend and consolidate the law relating to legal practitioners and to provide for the constitution of Bar Councils and an All-India Bar, unifying the legal profession under a single class of practitioners called 'advocates'
Create separate classes of pleaders, vakils, and barristers with no unification
Apply only to the Supreme Court of India
questions.src: Advocates Act 1961 — consolidated and unified the previously fragmented legal profession (pleaders, vakils, barristers, attorneys) into a single class of 'advocates', with State Bar Councils and the Bar Council of India as regulatory bodies

questions.q: Under the Advocates Act, 1961, a person seeking enrolment as an advocate must generally hold a recognised law degree and:
o: No further requirement is necessary

Apply for enrolment to the State Bar Council within whose jurisdiction they propose to practise, and fulfil other prescribed qualifications/conditions (such as being a citizen of India, subject to reciprocity provisions for foreign nationals, and being of a specified minimum age)
Automatically be enrolled without any application
Only be enrolled if recommended by a sitting High Court judge
questions.src: Advocates Act 1961, Section 24 — lays down the qualifications for enrolment as an advocate, including holding a law degree and applying to the relevant State Bar Council, among other conditions

questions.q: Under Section 33 of the Advocates Act, 1961, subject to specified exceptions, no person is entitled to practise in any court or before any authority/person unless they are:
o: A close relative of a sitting judge
Enrolled as an advocate under the Act, establishing the exclusive right of duly enrolled advocates to practise law in India
A retired police officer
Simply someone who has read law books independently, with no formal enrolment required
questions.src: Advocates Act 1961, Section 33 -- confers the exclusive right to practise law on persons enrolled as advocates under the Act, subject to limited statutory exceptions

questions.q: Under the Advocates Act, 1961, which of the following would generally constitute a disqualification affecting a person's enrolment or continuance as an advocate?
o: Having studied at a government law college

Being convicted of an offence involving moral turpitude, or engaging in full-time salaried employment inconsistent with the practice of law (subject to specified exceptions), among other disqualifying grounds specified in the Act/Rules
Living outside the city where they were enrolled
Being a woman
questions.src: Advocates Act 1961 and BCI Rules — disqualifying grounds include conviction for an offence involving moral turpitude and engaging in incompatible full-time employment, among others specified in the Act and Bar Council Rules

questions.q: A 'Solicitor', as historically recognised (notably in the Bombay and Calcutta High Courts), is generally distinguished from an ordinary advocate by the fact that solicitors traditionally:
o: Only argue cases in the Supreme Court and nowhere else

Primarily prepare and manage a case (paperwork, client interaction, briefing counsel) rather than arguing the matter in open court, which was traditionally done by a separate class of advocates/barristers whom the solicitor briefed
Have no connection to the legal profession at all
Are exclusively criminal lawyers
questions.src: Settled legal-profession history — the historical distinction (particularly in Bombay/Calcutta High Courts) between solicitors (case preparation, client management) and advocates/barristers (court advocacy), a distinction largely blurred in most of India post-Advocates Act 1961

questions.q: The 'Seven Lamps of Advocacy', a classical framework describing the essential qualities of a good advocate (associated with Judge Edward Abbott Parry), include qualities such as:
o: Wealth, aggression, and secrecy
Honesty, Courage, Industry, Wit, Eloquence, Judgment, and Fellowship, among the qualities traditionally identified as essential to the art and ethics of advocacy
Only physical strength and stamina
Only the ability to memorise legal codes verbatim
questions.src: 'The Seven Lamps of Advocacy' by Edward Abbott Parry — a classical work identifying qualities such as Honesty, Courage, Industry, Wit, Eloquence, Judgment, and Fellowship as foundational to ethical advocacy, widely referenced in Indian legal ethics curricula

questions.q: Among an advocate's foremost ethical duties towards the Court, as recognised under the Bar Council of India Rules, is the duty to:
o: Always agree with whatever the judge suggests, even if factually wrong

Act with dignity and self-respect while maintaining respect towards the Court, not to communicate with the judge privately regarding a pending case (ex parte communication), and to conduct themselves so as not to influence the Court's decision by improper means
Bribe court officials to expedite cases
Never appear in court without a specific written request from the client each time
questions.src: Bar Council of India Rules, Chapter II, Part VI (Standards of Professional Conduct and Etiquette) — 'Duty to the Court' includes maintaining respect and dignity, avoiding private/ex parte communication with the judge on pending matters, and not seeking to influence the court improperly

questions.q: An advocate's duty towards their client generally includes the duty to act with utmost good faith, and NOT to:
o: Accept any fee for services rendered

Adjust unreasonable delay in the case for personal benefit, withhold accounts/settle without client instructions, or act contrary to the client's legitimate interests, among other duties reflecting a fiduciary relationship
Ever advise a client on the merits of their case
Represent more than one client in their entire career
questions.src: Bar Council of India Rules — duty to the client is fiduciary in nature, requiring the advocate to act with utmost good faith, avoid conflicts of interest, and not act in a manner detrimental to the client's legitimate interests

questions.q: An advocate's duty towards the opposing party/opposing counsel, under the Bar Council of India Rules, generally requires the advocate to:
o: Use any means, however improper, to defeat the opposing party

Conduct the case fairly, refrain from unnecessary and unjustifiable communication with the opposing party (where represented by counsel) outside the knowledge of their counsel, and abstain from acting in a manner that involves deception or fraud against the opponent
Refuse to speak to opposing counsel under any circumstances
Automatically settle every case rather than proceed to trial
questions.src: Bar Council of India Rules — duty towards opponent requires fair conduct, avoiding fraudulent practices, and observing courtesy even in adversarial proceedings

questions.q: An advocate's ethical duty to render legal aid to the poor and needy is generally recognised as:
o: A purely optional matter with no professional expectation attached

An important professional and social obligation of the legal profession, reflected in both the Bar Council of India Rules' expectations and the broader constitutional/statutory framework for legal aid (e.g., through the Legal Services Authorities Act 1987)
A duty applicable only to government-employed lawyers
Prohibited under the Advocates Act 1961
questions.src: Settled professional ethics principle — rendering legal aid to those unable to afford it is regarded as an important obligation of the legal profession, aligned with Article 39A of the Constitution and the Legal Services Authorities Act 1987

questions.topic: Bar Council of India — Code of Ethics
questions.q: The 'Standards of Professional Conduct and Etiquette' governing advocates in India are laid down under:
o: The Indian Penal Code
Chapter II, Part VI of the Bar Council of India Rules (made under the Advocates Act 1961)
The Constitution of India directly, with no subordinate rules
Only informal, unwritten customs with no codified form
questions.src: Bar Council of India Rules, Chapter II, Part VI (framed under Section 49(1)(c) of the Advocates Act 1961) — codifies the Standards of Professional Conduct and Etiquette binding on all advocates

questions.q: Under Rule 36 of the Bar Council of India Rules, an advocate is generally prohibited from:
o: Ever appearing in court

Soliciting work or advertising, either directly or indirectly, whether by circulars, advertisements, touts, personal communication, interviews not warranted by personal relations, furnishing/inspiring newspaper comments, or procuring their photograph to be published in connection with cases they are engaged in
Charging any fee whatsoever for legal services
Wearing the prescribed advocate's dress in court
questions.src: Bar Council of India Rules, Rule 36 — the well-established prohibition on advertising and solicitation by advocates, aimed at preserving the dignity of the legal profession

questions.q: 'Professional misconduct' by an advocate, under the Advocates Act, 1961, is generally understood to encompass:
o: Only conduct that is also a criminal offence under the Indian Penal Code

Conduct unbefitting an advocate, whether in their professional or, in some cases, private capacity, that is likely to bring disrepute to the legal profession or is inconsistent with the standards of conduct expected of an advocate, though the Act itself does not exhaustively define the term
Only failure to pay Bar Council membership fees
Only conduct occurring inside a courtroom
questions.src: Advocates Act 1961 — 'professional misconduct' is not exhaustively defined in the Act, allowing Bar Councils/courts to determine on a case-by-case basis whether conduct is unbefitting an advocate and detracts from the profession's standards

questions.q: Under the Advocates Act, 1961, a complaint of professional misconduct against an advocate is generally first examined by:
o: The Supreme Court of India directly, in every single case without exception

The Disciplinary Committee of the State Bar Council (with further appeal to the Bar Council of India, and ultimately the Supreme Court), constituted under the Act to inquire into and decide complaints of misconduct
The local police station
The advocate's own client, with no independent body involved
questions.src: Advocates Act 1961, Sections 35-37 — establishes the disciplinary framework: State Bar Council Disciplinary Committee (first instance), appeal to Bar Council of India, and further appeal to the Supreme Court

questions.q: Upon finding an advocate guilty of professional misconduct, the Disciplinary Committee of a State Bar Council may, under Section 35 of the Advocates Act, 1961, impose punishments including:
o: Only a warning, with no other punishment possible
Reprimand, suspension from practice for a specified period, or removal of the advocate's name from the roll of advocates (effectively permanent debarment), depending on the severity of the misconduct
Only imprisonment, since fines are not permitted
Automatic and permanent disqualification with no possibility of any lesser punishment
questions.src: Advocates Act 1961, Section 35(3) — Disciplinary Committee may dismiss the complaint, reprimand the advocate, suspend them from practice for a specified period, or remove their name from the State roll, calibrated to the misconduct's severity

questions.topic: Transfer to Bar Council of India
questions.q: Under Section 36-B of the Advocates Act, 1961, if a State Bar Council's Disciplinary Committee fails to dispose of a complaint within a specified period, the proceedings are:
o: Automatically dismissed with no further action
Transferred to the Bar Council of India, which then has the disciplinary jurisdiction to proceed with the matter as if it were originally filed there
Transferred to the complainant's local police station
Referred to the President of India for a personal decision
questions.src: Advocates Act 1961, Section 36-B — mandates transfer of a State Bar Council's disciplinary proceeding to the Bar Council of India if not disposed of within one year of receipt of the complaint

questions.q: In P.D. Gupta v. Ram Murti, a leading case on professional misconduct, an advocate was found guilty of misconduct essentially because he:
o: Refused to accept a client's case

Purchased property that was the subject matter of ongoing litigation from a client, while aware of a genuine dispute over her identity/title, and made a profit from the transaction — conduct held to breach the fiduciary duty an advocate owes, including to the opposing party in the proceedings
Charged a fee that was too low for his services
Was late in filing court documents on one occasion
questions.src: P.D. Gupta v. Ram Murti and Anr. (Supreme Court) — advocate found guilty of professional misconduct for purchasing disputed litigation property from a client at undervalue for personal profit while aware of doubts over her claimed identity/title

questions.topic: Professional Misconduct — Case Law (Hikmat Ali Khan)
questions.q: In Hikmat Ali Khan v. Ishwar Prasad Arya (1997), the Supreme Court dealt with a case where an advocate had:
o: Failed to attend a client meeting

Assaulted the opposing party (a fellow advocate) with a knife during court proceedings, conduct which the Supreme Court held to be a very serious act of professional misconduct warranting the highest punishment of removal from the roll of advocates
Filed a case one day late
Charged excessive court fees to a client
questions.src: Hikmat Ali Khan v. Ishwar Prasad Arya (1997) — Supreme Court case where an advocate physically assaulted an opposing party/advocate; treated as grave professional misconduct warranting the most severe punishment

questions.topic: Contempt of Court and Professional Misconduct
questions.q: An advocate's conduct amounting to 'Contempt of Court' (e.g., wilful disobedience of a court order, or scandalising the court) can, in appropriate cases, ALSO give rise to proceedings for:
o: No other legal consequence at all beyond the contempt proceeding

Professional misconduct under the Advocates Act 1961, since such conduct reflects on the advocate's fitness to practise, meaning contempt and disciplinary proceedings can potentially run alongside or feed into each other depending on the facts
Automatic revocation of the advocate's law degree by the university
Nothing, since contempt of court has no bearing on professional standing
questions.src: Settled principle — conduct amounting to contempt of court can also constitute professional misconduct warranting separate disciplinary action under the Advocates Act 1961, since both concern the advocate's fitness and conduct befitting the profession

questions.q: The maintenance of proper accounts by an advocate, particularly regarding client funds received in a professional capacity, is generally considered:
o: Entirely optional, with no ethical significance
An important professional obligation, since an advocate holds client funds in a position of trust, and mismanagement or misappropriation of such funds constitutes serious professional misconduct
Relevant only to chartered accountants, not advocates
A matter governed exclusively by the Income Tax Act, with no bearing on legal ethics
questions.src: Settled principle of legal ethics and accountancy for lawyers — advocates hold client money in trust, and proper accounting/non-misappropriation of client funds is a core professional obligation, breach of which is serious misconduct

questions.q: In R.D. Saxena v. Balram Prasad Sharma, the Supreme Court held, in the context of an advocate's dealings with client files/documents upon termination of engagement, that an advocate:
o: May retain the client's case files indefinitely as a matter of right, regardless of unpaid fees

Does NOT have a general lien over the client's files/papers for unpaid fees, and cannot refuse to return them to the client on that ground, since case files/papers are not 'goods' over which such a lien can be claimed in this manner
Can destroy client files immediately upon non-payment of fees
Is legally required to charge no fee at all if the client is dissatisfied
questions.src: R.D. Saxena v. Balram Prasad Sharma (Supreme Court) — held that an advocate cannot retain a client's files as a lien for unpaid fees, since litigation papers are not 'goods' in the ordinary commercial sense, and withholding them would prejudice the client's case

questions.q: Among the important branches of accounting relevant to legal/professional practice, 'Financial Accounting' primarily deals with:
o: Only tax planning strategies

The recording, classifying, and summarising of financial transactions to prepare financial statements (like the balance sheet and profit/loss account) reflecting the financial position and performance of an entity/practice over a period
Only criminal financial fraud investigation
Only government budget allocation
questions.src: Settled accounting principle — financial accounting is the branch concerned with systematically recording transactions and preparing financial statements reflecting financial position and performance

questions.q: 'Bar-Bench Relations' refers to the professional relationship and mutual respect expected between:
o: Two rival law firms competing for the same client

Advocates (the 'Bar') and Judges (the 'Bench'), a relationship considered essential for the smooth and dignified administration of justice, requiring courtesy, cooperation, and mutual respect from both sides
Only senior advocates and junior advocates within the same firm
Only advocates and their own clients
questions.src: Settled principle of legal ethics — Bar-Bench relations denote the professional relationship between advocates and judges, essential to the dignified functioning of the justice system, requiring cooperation and mutual respect

questions.q: The Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, which is relevant to professional ethics in the context of an advocate's conduct towards the judiciary, generally distinguishes between:
o: No distinct categories of contempt exist under the Act

'Civil contempt' (wilful disobedience of a court order/undertaking) and 'Criminal contempt' (acts that scandalise the court, prejudice judicial proceedings, or interfere with the administration of justice)
Only contempt committed by government officials
Contempt applicable exclusively to the Supreme Court
questions.src: Contempt of Courts Act 1971, Section 2 — distinguishes civil contempt (wilful disobedience of orders/undertakings) from criminal contempt (scandalising the court, prejudicing proceedings, or obstructing justice administration)
